newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair has mandate he needs to be radical.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair has mandate he needs to be radical.

text.p: Tony Blair's landslide election victory has given Britain's Labour leader the mandate he craved to redeem his pledge to be a truly radical prime minister, analysts said on Friday.

With a huge majority in parliament of around 180, Blair can look forward confidently to at least two five-year terms unless the Conservatives quickly regroup and end once and for all their long-running civil war over Europe.

Labour rewrote the record books in sweeping to power for the first time since 1979 on a 10.2 percent swing of the votes -- twice the previous 5.2 percent record -- and history would improbably have to repeat itself to rob Blair of a second term.

But even without that safety net, analysts said Blair has a free hand to ram through controversial changes to Britain's constitution and -- if he chooses -- to strike a more positive stance on Europe.

"The Conservative party will find it very difficult to oppose a Labour government that has got such a whopping majority in the House of Commons," Ivor Crewe, politics professor at Essex University, said.

The difficulties that Major had steering government business through parliament in the last months of his administration, when his majority gradually evaporated into a minority, show how invaluable a fat majority can be. Margaret Thatcher only undertook her major economic reforms once she had won a 140-plus Conservative majority at the 1983 election.
Robin Cook, foreign secretary-in-waiting, dismissed the risk that the large majority would encourage Labour Euro-sceptics hostile to closer European ties to flout party discipline.

"In the context of a parliamentary Labour party of over 400, we're certainly not going to have any problem there... It's not going to be the case that you've got dissidents running off pursuing their own different issues," he said.

European leaders, including Germany Chancellor Helmut Kohl and French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, said Labour's victory was a sign that hostility to Europe did not win votes -- leading Euro-sceptic Michael Portillo, the outgoing defence secretary, headed the Conservatives' casualty list in losing his seat.

Although Blair struck a sceptical note during the campaign, he left himself much more room for manoeuvre than Major, whose warning that Labour was "dangerously" European fell on deaf ears, commentator Hugo Young wrote in the Guardian newspaper.
"What price... the continuation of a phobic posture toward the European Union?" he asked.
The Financial Times agreed that Blair's unprecedented majority meant he could afford to be bold. "On Europe, he has the freedom to chart a fresh course," the paper commented.

The wipe-out of the Conservatives in Scotland and Wales, where they lost all their seats, should also make it easier for Blair to drive through plans to set up a tax-raising parliament in Edinburgh and an assembly in Wales.

"The Conservatives have a real problem in reconstructing themselves as a national party. They are hardly there in urban Britain and not there in Scotland or Wales," political expert Peter Kellner said.
The chances of the Conservatives turning inward and becoming a rump English nationalist party could only grow if a looming leadership contest confirms a hardening of the party's Euro-scepticism.
That in turn could free up even more of the centre ground of politics that Blair has already largely captured in his single-minded remodelling of the party.
It was by gradually occupying the centre ground that Margaret Thatcher ensured four terms in office for her Conservative party. Blair must already be able to glimpse the same enticing prospect.
"It's not 2002 we're looking at -- it's 2017," a Labour official said as the scale of Blair's landslide finally sank in.
